bib.title: Fair prediction with disparate impact: A study of bias in recidivism prediction instruments
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv v1, stat.AP, 24 Oct 2016); published as Big Data 2017 (doi from caller, not in PDF)

question: Can a recidivism score that is free of predictive bias (calibrated across race) still produce unequal false positive and false negative rates and disparate impact when prevalence differs across groups?
hypothesis: Differences in FPR and FNR cited by ProPublica are a direct consequence of applying a predictively unbiased instrument to groups with different recidivism prevalence.
contributions: Make precise the connection between the psychometric notion of test fairness and error rates in classification.
Demonstrate how an RPI with different FPR and FNR between groups can lead to disparate impact when high-risk individuals receive stricter penalties.

method.summary: Algebraic derivation (eq 2.4, Props 3.1-3.2) plus descriptive plots on the ProPublica Broward County COMPAS data; no model is trained.
method.task: fairness analysis of recidivism risk scores

limits: Sample size, PPV by race and the cutoff behind the footnote-4 FPR/FNR are not stated in the text.
Only a simple binary-score, binary-penalty (MinMax) setting; says all salient features are present but non-binary analogs are not shown.
Analysis covers only use cases where high risk means a stricter penalty, not risk-reduction uses (e.g. PCRA).
Fairness is called a social and ethical concept; no recommendation on which criterion to pick, and the level of granularity for error balance is left to the decision maker.
Does not discuss rearrest as a proxy for reoffence or label bias; the outcome is called 2-year recidivism with no discussion of measurement. These are absences, not conceded limits.
Calibration claim for COMPAS rests on Fig 1 and a cited Flores et al. regression, no test reported.
This is arXiv v1; later versions differ (the target note quotes text and eq 2.6 not found here).

terms.definition: A score S is test-fair if it reflects the same likelihood of recidivism irrespective of group membership: P(Y=1|S=s,R=b)=P(Y=1|S=s,R=w) for all s.
settings where a penalty policy has unintended disproportionate adverse impact on a particular group
